pos: n. (the Scottish kingdom between Forth and Tay, holding St Andrews, where Patrick Hamilton was burned in 1528 and George Wishart in 1546)
etymology: Scottish Gaelic Fìobha, of uncertain derivation, traditionally from Fib, one of the seven sons of Cruithne in the Pictish origin legend.
biblical_def: Fife is the peninsula between the Firths of Forth and Tay, called a kingdom from its old Pictish standing, and its cathedral city of St Andrews was the ecclesiastical capital of Scotland. The Scottish Reformation was lit there twice by fire. Patrick Hamilton, a young abbot of noble family who had studied at Paris and Marburg and come home preaching justification by faith, was burned before St Salvator's College in February 1528; the burning was slow and botched and was watched by students, and the saying went round that the reek of Master Patrick Hamilton had infected as many as it blew upon. George Wishart, who had taught the Greek New Testament and preached through Angus and Ayrshire, was burned before the castle in March 1546 with Cardinal Beaton watching from a window; Beaton was murdered in that castle three months later, and John Knox, who had carried a sword for Wishart, preached his first sermon in the parish church of St Andrews in 1547. The dictionary records the two martyrs and not the assassination, and holds that the first did the work the second only hindered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion; reek as smoke or vapour; to infect as to taint; a cardinal as a dignitary of the Roman church; and justification as the act of absolving from guilt.
webster_full: MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defence of the Christian faith, or of any cause he believes to be true.
REEK, n. Vapour; steam; smoke; as the reek of a fire or of a chimney.
INFECT, v.t. To taint with disease; to communicate bad qualities to; to corrupt; to affect with a kindred quality.
CARDINAL, n. An ecclesiastical prince in the Roman church, who has a voice in the conclave at the election of a pope.
JUSTIFICATION, n. In theology, remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; the act of acquitting.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
corruption_summary: Scottish kingdom between Forth and Tay whose cathedral city of St Andrews burned Patrick Hamilton in 1528 and George Wishart in 1546, after which Knox preached his first sermon there in 1547.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the doctrine the fires were lit to protect, which was the whole scheme of merit: that a man is made righteous by a grace infused and cooperated with rather than by a righteousness imputed to him, and that the church disposes of the means. Hamilton had read Luther at Marburg and came home with the article the Roman system cannot survive, and he was burned for it at twenty-four. John's vision puts such men where the dictionary puts them: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9). Paul warns that this is the ordinary rate, not an aberration of one century: “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12).

The second paragraph names a corruption on the Protestant side, and names it against men whose cause the dictionary holds. Cardinal Beaton was murdered in his own castle in May 1546 by a party of Fife lairds in revenge for Wishart, and the deed was defended afterward as a judgment executed by private men. It was murder. Wishart's death had already begun to convert the country; Beaton's death gave the regent a siege, a French fleet and a pretext, sent Knox to the galleys, and set the Reformation back years. The psalm describes the church's true condition and expects no sword in its hand: “for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22). Micah supplies the right expectation under defeat, which is patience and not reprisal: “when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me” (Mic 7:8). The reek of Master Patrick Hamilton did more than the daggers in the castle.

Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay, to butcher; “of them that were slain for the word of God”, Revelation 6:9.

“all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12) — the ordinary rate, not an aberration.
“when I fall, I shall arise” (Mic 7:8) — patience, against the daggers in the castle.

pos: n. (the Scottish district about Edinburgh where the National Covenant was subscribed at Greyfriars in 1638)
etymology: From the British kingdom name Lleuddiniawn, traditionally the land of Lot or Leudonus; applied to the country south of the Forth.
biblical_def: Lothian is the Scottish district lying south of the Firth of Forth, with Edinburgh at its centre, and it is where the Scottish church transacted its public business. Knox was minister of St Giles from 1559; the General Assembly met in the city; the Court of Session and the Scottish parliament sat there. Its great day is the twenty-eighth of February 1638, when, after Charles I had imposed a new service book on Scotland the previous year without the consent of assembly or parliament, the National Covenant was subscribed in Greyfriars kirk and kirkyard by the nobility, gentry, burgesses and ministers of the kingdom, and then carried through the country for subscription. It bound the subscribers to maintain the reformed religion as settled, and to resist the innovations; it did not claim to make a new religion but to hold an old one. The Glasgow Assembly of the following November abolished the bishops and the service book. Lothian also saw the Tron riot, the trials of Covenanters in the Grassmarket and the executions of Guthrie and Argyll. The dictionary honours the Covenant and names the error that grew out of it, which was to treat a national bond as the church's foundation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement; to subscribe as to sign with one's own hand; a vow as a solemn promise to God; to perform as to carry out; and innovation as the introduction of something new.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract.
SUBSCRIBE, v.t. To sign with one's own hand; to give consent to something written by signing one's name.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a solemn promise to perform some act, or make some gift or sacrifice.
PERFORM, v.t. To do; to execute; to accomplish; to fulfil, as a promise or covenant.
INNOVATION, n. Change made by the introduction of something new; a novelty, especially in religion or government.
scriptures: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;

And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
corruption_summary: Scottish district about Edinburgh where the National Covenant was subscribed at Greyfriars on 28 February 1638 and carried through the kingdom, after Charles I imposed a service book without assembly or parliament.
corruption_paragraphs: The lawful part of the business is the covenant itself, and the dictionary defends it against the common charge that a nation has no business binding itself in religion. Scripture records exactly this act twice and commends it both times. Asa's generation “entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul” (2Ch 15:12); Josiah stood by a pillar and “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments” (2Ki 23:3), and all the people stood to it. The Scots in 1638 did what these did: they bound themselves to an obedience already commanded, against an innovation imposed by a prince without the consent of the church. That is not sedition and it is not novelty.

The corruption to name is what grew out of it afterward. A bond subscribed by a nation came in time to be treated as though it were the ground of the church's standing, so that men asked whether a kingdom was covenanted rather than whether a congregation held the faith, and the Solemn League of 1643 attached to it the politics of a war. A vow binds the man who makes it, and Scripture is severe about that: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4). But a vow is not a gospel, and a nation's subscription saves nobody. Joshua's setting of the matter is the one the dictionary keeps, because it ends with a household rather than a kingdom: “but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15).

roots_lines: Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to enquire after; “a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers”, 2 Chronicles 15:12.
Hebrew karath-sense of cutting a covenant in Josiah's act — “made a covenant before the LORD”, 2 Kings 23:3.
Hebrew 'amad (H5975) — to stand, to take one's stand; “And all the people stood to the covenant”, 2 Kings 23:3.
Hebrew nadar (H5087) — to vow, to promise solemnly; “When thou vowest a vow unto God”, Ecclesiastes 5:4.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house, a household; “but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD”, Joshua 24:15.
usage: “a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 15:12) — Greyfriars, 28 February 1638.
“And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3) — the Covenant carried through the kingdom.
“but as for me and my house” (Jos 24:15) — a household, where a kingdom's bond cannot reach.

pos: n. (the south-western Scottish county where the Lollards of Kyle were summoned in 1494 and which became the heartland of the Covenanters)
etymology: From Ayr, from the river name, probably Brittonic meaning a strong or clear stream; with Scots shire.
biblical_def: Ayrshire is the south-western Scottish county on the Firth of Clyde, divided into the old districts of Cunninghame, Kyle and Carrick, and no county in Britain held a longer unbroken record of religious dissent. In 1494 some thirty lairds and gentlemen of Kyle were summoned before James IV and the Archbishop of Glasgow on charges of heresy; Knox lists their articles, which include denial of the mass as a sacrifice, of purgatory, of indulgences, of image worship and of papal authority, and reports that one of them, Adam Reid of Barskimming, answered the king so freely that the business was dropped. These were the Lollards of Kyle, and they were in the same county where, a century and a half later, John Welsh preached at Ayr, where Alexander Peden kept the fields, where the Mauchline rising gathered, and where more Covenanters were killed between 1666 and 1688 than in any other shire. The dictionary records the continuity, and marks that the articles of 1494 and the testimonies of 1680 are substantially the same articles.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Lollard as one of a sect of early reformers; an article as a particular of a confession; to summon as to cite to appear; a testimony as a solemn declaration; and to contend as to strive in argument.
webster_full: LOLLARD, n. One of a sect of early reformers in Germany and England; a follower of Wickliffe.
ARTICLE, n. A single clause or item of an account, a confession or a charge; a distinct proposition.
SUMMON, v.t. To call, cite or notify by authority to appear at a place specified, or to attend to some duty.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing a fact; witness; evidence.
CONTEND, v.i. To strive in debate; to dispute earnestly; to struggle in opposition.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Heb 12:4
Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.
corruption_summary: South-western Scottish county where some thirty lairds of Kyle were summoned for heresy in 1494 and which later lost more Covenanters than any other shire between 1666 and 1688.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the articles of the faith are stable and that a people which holds them will hold them under any century's pressure. The Lollards of Kyle in 1494 denied the sacrifice of the mass, purgatory, indulgences, the worship of images and the pope's authority; the Covenanters of Carrick and Kyle in 1680 denied the same things and added a denial of the king's supremacy over the church. That is one doctrine in two centuries, held by farmers and lairds in the same parishes. The standard they both appealed to is the one Isaiah gives, which is available to a ploughman as much as to a doctor: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

The second thing to recover is the method such people used, which was examination rather than enthusiasm. Adam Reid of Barskimming answered a king and an archbishop to their faces out of the text, and the Ayrshire societies of the sixteen-eighties kept to a discipline of reading, conference and prayer. The Bereans are the commended pattern, having “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). The duty is stated as a struggle over a fixed deposit, to “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). And the measure actually exacted in that county is the measure Hebrews names as the furthest point, which most of us have not reached: “Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” (Heb 12:4). In Ayrshire a great many did.

Hebrew te'udah (H8584) — a testimony, an attestation; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to investigate; “and searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.

Greek antagonizomai (G464) — to struggle against; “striving against sin”, Hebrews 12:4.

“and searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — the Ayrshire societies of the sixteen-eighties.
“Ye have not yet resisted unto blood” (Heb 12:4) — in this county a great many did.

pos: n. (the south-western Scottish province of Whithorn and Anwoth, where Samuel Rutherford served the parish he wrote his letters from)
etymology: From Gaelic Gall-Ghaidhil, the foreign Gaels, the Norse-Gaelic population of the south-west; the province name follows.
biblical_def: Galloway is the south-western province of Scotland, the old lordship covering Wigtownshire and the Stewartry of Kirkcudbright, remote, Gaelic-speaking into the later Middle Ages and very hard to govern. Whithorn in its western peninsula holds the site of Ninian's mission in the fifth century, the earliest Christian foundation in Scotland, and became a cathedral priory and the chief Scottish pilgrimage. Its importance in the dictionary is the parish of Anwoth. Samuel Rutherford was settled there in 1627, a tiny upland charge by the Fleet, and ministered in it for nine years until he was deposed and confined to Aberdeen for refusing conformity; from that exile he wrote the letters to his Anwoth people and to others that were collected after his death and have never been out of print among the Reformed. He returned in 1638, went to St Andrews as professor, sat in the Westminster Assembly, and wrote Lex, Rex. Galloway afterwards suffered heavily in the persecution. The dictionary records Anwoth as the proof that the size of a charge has no relation to the reach of a ministry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister having the care of a church; a hireling as one who serves for wages; a flock as a congregation; to scatter as to disperse; and an overseer as one who superintends.
webster_full: PASTOR, n. A shepherd; a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages; a mercenary; one who serves for gain only.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation.
SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; in Scripture, a bishop or pastor of a church.
scriptures: Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened.
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: South-western Scottish province of Whithorn and the Stewartry, where Samuel Rutherford served the upland parish of Anwoth from 1627 and from his Aberdeen confinement wrote the letters collected after his death.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the hireling ministry, which Galloway knew in both forms, the absentee holder of a remote charge and the conforming minister put in over a congregation that had not called him. Scripture's language for this is harsh and the dictionary does not file it down. Zechariah pronounces a woe “to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock!” (Zec 11:17), promising the withering of the arm and the darkening of the eye that would have served. Our Lord distinguishes the hireling by what he does when the cost arrives: he “seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12). The men put into Galloway parishes after 1662 in the room of the ejected were in that position whatever their private character, and the people of the province, who walked miles past their own kirks to hear the outed ministers, understood it perfectly.

The second paragraph names the alternative, which Anwoth supplies. Rutherford had a handful of families on a hillside and was out of his parish more than in it, and his nine years there have fed the Reformed church for four centuries. The promise of Jeremiah is of a particular kind of man, not of a sufficient number of men: “I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15). Paul grounds the office in the purchase price of the flock and makes that the reason for vigilance: “feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). The dictionary notes that Rutherford's letters were written to people he had been forbidden to see, which is the ordinary way such books get written, and that a parish of that size would today be judged unviable.

roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7462) — to pasture, to tend, to shepherd; “pastors according to mine heart”, Jeremiah 3:15.
Hebrew 'elil-sense of worthlessness in Zechariah's woe — “Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock!”, Zechariah 11:17.
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired servant, a hireling; “he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd”, John 10:12.
Greek skorpizo (G4650) — to scatter, to disperse; “and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep”, John 10:12.
Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to acquire, to purchase for oneself; “which he hath purchased with his own blood”, Acts 20:28.

“Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock!” (Zec 11:17) — the conformists put in after 1662.
“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — the ground of a pastor's vigilance.

pos: n. (the Clyde valley county where the Covenanters won at Drumclog and were destroyed at Bothwell Bridge within three weeks of 1679)
etymology: From Lanark, from Brittonic llanerch, a forest clearing or glade; with Scots shire.
biblical_def: Lanarkshire is the county of the upper and middle Clyde, running from the moors above Leadhills down through Lanark and Hamilton to Glasgow. It was the central ground of the armed phase of the Covenanting struggle. On the first of June 1679 a field meeting at Drumclog in the parish of Avondale was attacked by John Graham of Claverhouse with a troop of dragoons; the Covenanters, warned and posted behind a bog, broke his horse and drove him off, the only clear victory they ever had. Within three weeks their numbers had swollen and their counsels had split between the men who would accept the king's authority and the extreme party, and on the twenty-second of June some five thousand of them were routed at Bothwell Bridge near Hamilton by Monmouth with regular troops and artillery; several hundred were killed, twelve hundred taken, and many transported or drowned off Orkney. Richard Cameron and Donald Cargill carried the testimony on alone afterward. The dictionary records the three weeks together, because they are the clearest demonstration in British history that a righteous cause does not sanctify a military remedy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as a private or unlawful assembly for worship; a dragoon as a mounted soldier; a rout as a total defeat; a chariot as a car of war; and carnal as fleshly.
webster_full: CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; appropriately, a secret or unlawful assembly for religious worship.
DRAGOON, n. A soldier or musketeer who serves on horseback or on foot as occasion requires.
ROUT, n. The breaking or defeat of an army or band of troops; a total defeat and disorderly flight.
CHARIOT, n. A carriage of pleasure or of state; a car of war used by the ancients in battle.
CARNAL, a. Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; sensual.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Clyde valley county where a field meeting beat Claverhouse at Drumclog on 1 June 1679 and where some five thousand Covenanters were routed at Bothwell Bridge three weeks later.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is a corruption of our own side, and the dictionary names it as plainly here as anywhere in the corpus. The Covenanters' cause was right: the king had no headship over Christ's church, the ejected ministers were lawfully called, and the field meetings were worship and not sedition. The resort to arms was wrong, and it destroyed them. Drumclog bred confidence, three weeks of swelling numbers bred division, and Bothwell Bridge finished the organised movement in a single morning. Paul states the character of the church's armoury in a parenthesis that leaves no room for dragoons: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). Christ's word in the garden is both a prohibition and a prediction: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).

The second paragraph sets out what the dictionary thinks should have been done instead, because a rebuke without an alternative is cheap. The societies ought to have gone on doing what they were doing at Drumclog before the dragoons came, which was meeting to hear the Word in the open and bearing the penalty. That is costly and it is not passive. The psalmist draws the line where the dictionary draws it: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Solomon grants the duty of preparation and removes the outcome from human hands: “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). Cameron and Cargill, who kept the testimony on foot after Bothwell with a handful of men and no army at all, did more for it than five thousand did at the bridge, and both were killed within two years.

Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; “The horse is prepared against the day of battle”, Proverbs 21:31.
Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668) — deliverance, safety, victory; “but safety is of the LORD”, Proverbs 21:31.
Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal”, 2 Corinthians 10:4.
Greek machaira (G3162) — a short sword, a dagger; “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword”, Matthew 26:52.

“but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31) — Bothwell Bridge, 22 June 1679.
“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) — Cameron and Cargill on foot afterward.

pos: n. (the Clyde county of Paisley, where seven people were executed for witchcraft in 1697 in the last mass witch burning in western Europe)
etymology: From Renfrew, probably Brittonic rhyn frwd, the point by the current, where the Cart meets the Clyde; with Scots shire.
biblical_def: Renfrewshire is the county on the south bank of the lower Clyde, with Paisley as its town and its great Cluniac abbey, founded in 1163 and the burial place of the Stewarts. It suffered with the rest of the west in the persecution, and its weavers were later famous for radical politics. Its episode in the dictionary is the Paisley witch trials. In 1696 Christian Shaw, the eleven-year-old daughter of the laird of Bargarran, began to exhibit fits, to vomit pins, hair and coal, and to name her tormentors; a commission was appointed, some twenty-four people were accused, and in June 1697 seven of them, including an old woman and a boy, were strangled and burned on the Gallow Green at Paisley. It was the last mass execution for witchcraft in western Europe. Christian Shaw grew up to establish the Bargarran thread industry. The dictionary names the proceedings as a judicial murder done by Presbyterians, carried out under a commission of the Scottish Privy Council with ministers attending, and it names the error that made it possible, which was the acceptance of a child's accusations as evidence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines witchcraft as the practices of witches; credulity as a disposition to believe on slight evidence; evidence as that which proves; to try as to examine by a test; and to lean as to rest upon for support.
webster_full: WITCHCRAFT, n. The practices of witches; sorcery; enchantments; intercourse with evil spirits.
CREDULITY, n. Easiness of belief; a disposition or readiness to believe without sufficient evidence.
EVIDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perceptions.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to prove by a test; to subject to a trial in order to determine the quality of a thing.
LEAN, v.i. To incline; to rest or rely for support; to depend or confide.
scriptures: Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Clyde county of Paisley and its Cluniac abbey, where seven people were strangled and burned on the Gallow Green in June 1697 on an eleven-year-old girl's accusations, the last mass witch execution in western Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is ours, and the dictionary will not shelter it behind the age. Scotland in 1697 was a Presbyterian country with a reformed church, a parish school in most parishes and a learned ministry, and it strangled and burned seven of its own people, one of them a boy, on the testimony of a girl who vomited pins. Ministers sat on the commission and preached at the executions. Scripture does treat sorcery as real and forbidden, and the dictionary does not take the modern line that nothing at all was ever there to be dealt with; Ephesus produced a bonfire of magical books, and it is worth marking who lit it, for “Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19). The owners burned their own books. Nobody was burned with them.

The second paragraph names the mechanism of the failure, which was evidential and therefore a failure of doctrine. The church is commanded to test claims, not to receive them: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1), and a tribunal that accepts the fits and namings of a child has abandoned the test altogether. The standard by which a spiritual claim is judged is a written one, and this is exactly what the Bargarran commission set aside: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Behind the whole affair lies the sin Solomon forbids, the trusting of one's own judgment at the moment it is least reliable: “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5). The dictionary records the seven of the Gallow Green as a standing warning that a sound confession does not by itself make a church just.

pos: n. (the East Lothian burgh reckoned John Knox's birthplace and the parish of John Brown, author of the Self-Interpreting Bible)
etymology: Old English Hadinton, the settlement of Hada's people; the county town of East Lothian on the Tyne.
biblical_def: Haddington is the county town of East Lothian, standing on the Scottish Tyne, and its great parish church of St Mary was called the Lamp of Lothian. John Knox was born in or near the burgh about 1514, the son of modest parents, and was educated at its school. Two centuries later the town gave the Reformed church a second man of a very different kind. John Brown, a herd boy from Carpow who taught himself Greek and Hebrew while watching sheep and was once suspected of having got his learning from the devil, became minister of the Secession congregation at Haddington in 1751 and professor of divinity to the Associate Synod, and served the one charge for thirty-six years. His Self-Interpreting Bible, published in 1778, surrounded the text with notes, summaries and cross-references drawn out of Scripture itself, and it went into countless Scottish and American households; his Dictionary of the Holy Bible did the same work in another form. The dictionary records both men, and marks that the burgh's two contributions to the Reformed church were a reformer and a commentator, and that the second was a self-taught shepherd.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inspiration as the supernatural influence of the Spirit; a commentary as an exposition; entrance as the act of entering; to accomplish as to complete; and to expound as to lay open the meaning.
webster_full: INSPIRATION, n. The supernatural influence of the Spirit of God on the human mind, by which prophets and apostles were qualified to deliver truth.
COMMENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation or illustration of a book or writing.
ENTRANCE, n. The act of entering; the power of entering; the opening or avenue by which a place is entered.
ACCOMPLISH, v.t. To complete; to finish entirely; to execute; to fulfil, as a prophecy or promise.
EXPOUND, v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: East Lothian burgh reckoned John Knox's birthplace about 1514 and the thirty-six-year charge of John Brown, the self-taught herd boy whose Self-Interpreting Bible was published in 1778.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Brown put in his title, that Scripture interprets Scripture. His Bible surrounded the text with material drawn out of the rest of the text, so that a reader with no library and no Latin could follow a doctrine through the canon and check it. That method rests on a conviction about the book's single authorship, that “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16); if one Author stands behind the whole, then the parts explain each other, and no external authority is needed to unlock them.

The second thing to recover is the dignity of the plain reader, which is the whole point of a self-interpreting Bible and the reason a herd boy could produce one. The psalmist claims an effect for the bare entrance of the words that requires no qualification in the hearer: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). The office of the minister in that scheme is Ezra's and Nehemiah's, to read and open rather than to mediate, for they “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). And the confidence that such labour is not wasted rests on the word's own guarantee: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). Brown was suspected of getting his Greek from the devil because nobody could believe a shepherd had got it from a book; the dictionary notes that the suspicion is a fair measure of how low the expectation of ordinary men had sunk, and that his Bible was published to raise it.

Hebrew pethi (H6612) — simple, untaught; “it giveth understanding unto the simple”, Psalm 119:130.

“it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130) — a herd boy suspected of devilish learning.
“gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — the minister's office, Brown's method.

pos: n. (the Fife fishing burgh whose minister James Melville fed and sent home the shipwrecked Spaniards of the Armada in 1588)
etymology: From Gaelic or Brittonic elements, probably an sruthair, the stream; the East Neuk burgh is divided into Easter and Wester Anstruther.
biblical_def: Anstruther is the fishing burgh of the East Neuk of Fife, and the scene of one of the best-attested acts of Christian charity in Scottish history. James Melville, nephew of Andrew Melville and minister of nearby Kilrenny, recorded in his diary what happened in the autumn of 1588. A great Spanish ship of the scattered Armada, the Saint Andrew of the squadron of Juan Gomez de Medina, was driven into the Forth in a wretched condition, and her commander came ashore at Anstruther and asked for mercy. The town had been expecting invasion, had prayed against the Armada and had every reason to hate the men; Melville met them, preached to them, and the burgh took in some two hundred and sixty starving and sick Spaniards, lodged and fed them for several weeks, and then provided a ship to carry them home. Gomez de Medina afterward, meeting Anstruther merchants at Cadiz whose vessel had been seized, intervened for them and had them released and sent home with his thanks. The dictionary records the episode without embellishment, because it is the plainest Scottish illustration of mercy shown where the law of war allowed none.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mercy as tenderness shewn to an offender; an enemy as one who is hostile; succour as help in distress; humanity as the kind feelings of man; and to requite as to repay.
webster_full: MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
ENEMY, n. A foe; an adversary; one who is hostile; in war, the opposing army or nation.
SUCCOUR, n. Aid; help; assistance; particularly, assistance that relieves and delivers from difficulty or distress.
HUMANITY, n. The peculiar nature of man; the kind feelings, dispositions and sympathies of man.
REQUITE, v.t. To repay; to return an equivalent in good or evil; to recompense; to retaliate.
scriptures: Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
Jam 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Hos 6:6
For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
corruption_summary: Fife fishing burgh whose minister James Melville met the shipwrecked Spaniards of the Armada in 1588, and which lodged and fed some two hundred and sixty of them before providing a ship to send them home.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that mercy to an enemy is a duty and not a luxury of the strong, and that it is commanded precisely where nothing recommends it. Anstruther in 1588 had prayed publicly against the Armada, expected to be invaded by it, and knew what Spain had done in the Low Countries; the men who came ashore represented a power that burned Protestants as policy. The town fed them. Our Lord's rebuke to the disciples who wanted a village destroyed names the temper that would have done otherwise: “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55). James puts the reason in a sentence that will not be argued with: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20).

The second thing to recover is that this is not sentiment set against doctrine. Melville did not conceal what he believed; by his own account he preached to the Spaniards and told them plainly what he thought of their religion and of their expedition, and then housed them for weeks. Mercy and plainness went together, which is how Scripture pairs them: what the LORD requires is “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8), three things in one clause, not a choice among them. The order of God's own preference is stated by Hosea, “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos 6:6). That a Spanish commander afterward repaid the burgh by freeing its merchants at Cadiz is a providence and not the reason for the act; the dictionary records it because Melville recorded it, and because it is the rarest kind of footnote in the history of that war.

“to do justly, and to love mercy” (Mic 6:8) — Melville preaching to them and housing them both.
“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6) — two hundred and sixty Spaniards fed and sent home.

pos: n. (the Ayrshire parish of the great communion seasons and of the Covenanters' rising of 1648 on Mauchline Moor)
etymology: Gaelic magh linne, the plain by the pool, from magh, a plain, and linne, a pool or waterfall.
biblical_def: Mauchline is the Ayrshire parish in the district of Kyle, with a castle that had been a cell of Melrose Abbey and a kirkyard that holds the graves of four Covenanters hanged at Edinburgh in 1685 and brought home. In June 1648 some two thousand armed men of the west, protesting against the Engagement by which the Scots parliament had contracted to send an army for Charles I, gathered on Mauchline Moor and were dispersed by Middleton's cavalry after a skirmish; it was one of the earliest of the western risings. The parish is better known for its communion seasons, the Scottish sacramental occasions at which several ministers preached over four or five days to thousands gathered in the open around the tables, with fast day, preparation, the Sabbath of the supper and a day of thanksgiving. The crowds, the tents and the behaviour at their edges were satirised by Robert Burns, who lived in the parish, in The Holy Fair of 1785. The dictionary defends the communion season as a lawful and weighty ordinance, and allows that the satire had something real to work on.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a communion as fellowship and the celebration of the Lord's supper; a token as a sign; a tent as a portable lodge; to prepare as to make ready; and decently as in a becoming manner.
webster_full: COMMUNION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; the celebration of the Lord's supper.
TOKEN, n. A sign; something intended to represent or indicate another thing; a mark; in Scotland, a metal piece admitting to the Lord's table.
TENT, n. A pavilion or portable lodge consisting of canvas or other cloth stretched and sustained by poles.
PREPARE, v.t. To fit, adapt or qualify for a particular purpose, end, use or employment; to make ready.
DECENTLY, adv. In a decent or becoming manner; with propriety of behaviour; suitably.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: Ayrshire parish in Kyle where two thousand western men were dispersed on Mauchline Moor in June 1648, and whose open-air communion seasons drew thousands and were satirised by Burns in 1785.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary defends the communion season first, because the modern instinct is to find it excessive. Several days of preaching, a fast day, a day of preparation, the supper itself and a day of thanksgiving, with tokens distributed to the examined and tables served in relays, is not an invention of enthusiasm but a serious attempt to obey two commands at once: to continue “stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42), and not to forsake “the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25). A church that reduces the supper to ten minutes at the end of a service has not become more spiritual than Mauchline; it has become less careful.

The corruption to name is the one Burns saw, and the dictionary grants it rather than denying it. A gathering of thousands in a field for four days collects a fair, and the drink, the courting and the preaching rivalry at the margins of the Holy Fair were real; so was the danger that the occasion itself became the religion, attended annually as a custom by people who were strangers to the thing commemorated. Where that happens the ordinance falls under the Lord's own word about observance resting on habit and human prescription: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The remedy is not abolition but order, and Paul supplies the rule for exactly this kind of large and loosely managed assembly: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). The dictionary adds that Burns was a parishioner and knew what he was describing, and that a satire a church cannot answer is usually a satire a church has earned.

“in vain they do worship me” (Mat 15:9) — what Burns saw at the edges of the Holy Fair.

pos: n. (the East Lothian burgh where Cromwell destroyed the Scottish covenanting army on 3 September 1650)
etymology: Gaelic dùn bàrr, the fort on the summit or point, from dùn, a fort, and bàrr, a top.
biblical_def: Dunbar is the East Lothian burgh on the coast east of Edinburgh, and twice a decisive battle was fought there. In 1296 Edward I's army broke the Scots and opened the Wars of Independence. The second is the one that concerns the dictionary. In 1650 Cromwell invaded Scotland against a nation that had crowned Charles II and bound itself by the Solemn League; David Leslie manoeuvred him into a corner at Dunbar with a sick and starving army of eleven thousand against a Scottish force of twice that number holding the high ground of Doon Hill. Then the Scots came down, pressed by their own ministers and committee of estates to finish the business; Cromwell saw it and said that God had delivered them into his hands. On the third of September his army attacked at dawn, broke the Scottish right, and destroyed the army in an hour, with three thousand killed and ten thousand taken. The dictionary records what both sides did with the result, since each read it as God's verdict on its own covenant, and neither reading was lawful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lot as that which falls by chance or providence; obedience as submission to authority; a chariot as a car of war; to prepare as to make ready; and a prince as a sovereign.
webster_full: LOT, n. That which, in human speech, is called chance; the decision of chance or divine providence by casting lots.
OBEDIENCE, n. Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law and rule prescribed as a duty.
CHARIOT, n. A carriage of state or pleasure; a car of war used by the ancients in battle.
PREPARE, v.t. To fit, adapt or qualify for a particular purpose; to make ready; to provide.
PRINCE, n. A sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state; a chief in rank.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Isa 31:1

Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
corruption_summary: East Lothian burgh where Cromwell destroyed a covenanting army of twice his numbers on 3 September 1650, three thousand killed and ten thousand taken, after the Scots came down from Doon Hill.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the reading of a battle as a divine verdict on a doctrine, and the dictionary names it on both sides because both sides did it. Cromwell declared that God had delivered the Scots into his hands and drew from Dunbar a confirmation of the whole English cause, Independency and the regicide included. The Scots, having lost, concluded in the Western Remonstrance that the defeat was a judgment for having crowned an ungodly king, and the kirk split over it into Resolutioners and Protesters for a generation. Neither inference was available to them. God's hand in the outcome is not in doubt, for “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33); but a providence tells a man what happened, not what to believe.

The second paragraph names the fault that lost the field, and it was a religious fault before it was a military one. Leslie had Cromwell beaten by position and starvation, and the ministers and the committee of estates pressed him off the hill because they wanted the deliverance to be visible and complete. That is the demand for a sign dressed as zeal, and Samuel's word to a king who had improved on his instructions covers it exactly: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). Isaiah pronounces a woe on the calculation that puts its confidence in the strength of an arrangement, on those who “trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 31:1). And the thing both armies were ultimately fighting over, the person of a king, is the thing Scripture most plainly forbids resting on: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). Ten thousand Scots were taken in an hour, and many of them died in Durham cathedral.
